edges.description: Reduced availability of the regulatory/structural isoform could alter complex IV function in susceptible tissues; normal fibroblast enzymology prevents assuming a universal deficit.
An attenuated expression response may limit adaptation under stress; the affected-organ consequences were not measured.
A tissue-specific metabolic defect is a proposed cause of pancreatic degeneration; intervening injury pathways are unknown.
The disease association links COX4I2 to erythroid pathology, but the cell-autonomous metabolic mechanism has not been established.
The original report proposes altered osteoclast function as an explanation for skull thickening.
Loss of exocrine tissue accompanies markedly reduced digestive enzyme output.
Loss of pancreatic parenchyma appears as atrophy on imaging.
Reduced pancreatic enzyme delivery impairs digestion and absorption of dietary fat.
Undigested dietary fat contributes to fatty stools.
Exocrine dysfunction causes malabsorption of fat-soluble nutrients.
Poor nutrient absorption contributes to early growth failure; growth can improve with enzyme treatment.
Vitamin E was low when enzyme replacement was withdrawn.
Impaired coagulation accompanied vitamin malabsorption off enzymes; specific factor assays were not reported.
Abnormal erythroid maturation contributes to anemia; the relative contribution of peripheral destruction remains uncertain.
Megaloblastic and multinucleated precursors document abnormal erythroid maturation.
The marrow expands its erythroid compartment despite anemia.
Reduced resorption is a proposed explanation for parietal thickening, not an experimentally established intermediate.
